content:
If you need equipment such as a walking frame, commode, raised toilet seat, perching stool or wheelchair for a short time — after a hospital stay, an operation, a fall or a bad flare — you can often borrow it rather than buy it. Equipment you are assessed as needing is free from the council or NHS community equipment service, usually after an occupational therapist or physiotherapist assessment; ask the hospital team before discharge or ask your council for a needs assessment. Charities such as the British Red Cross hire out wheelchairs, and if you buy, ask a therapist what suits you first and check second-hand items carefully. Return loaned equipment when you no longer need it.

This guide is about getting equipment quickly for a short spell. For choosing everyday gadgets you will keep, see how to choose arthritis-friendly products, and for sticks, rollators and wheelchairs in more depth, see choosing mobility aids. For permanent changes to your home, such as a stairlift or level-access shower, see Disabled Facilities Grants.

When short-term equipment helps

  • Coming home from hospital after an operation such as a hip or knee replacement, or after an illness that has left you weaker.
  • After a fall, while you get your confidence and strength back.
  • During a bad arthritis flare, when getting to the toilet, washing or dressing is suddenly much harder.
  • For a trip or a family event, when you need a wheelchair for distance.

Common items include walking frames and rollators, commodes, raised toilet seats and toilet frames, perching stools, bath boards, chair and bed raisers, grab rails and wheelchairs.

Route 1: free equipment from the council or NHS

The NHS says equipment and small adaptations will be provided free if you are assessed as needing them. Most areas have a community equipment service run by the council and the NHS that delivers, fits and collects equipment.

  • Before you leave hospital: ask the ward team, physiotherapist or occupational therapist what equipment you will need at home and who will arrange it. Ask for it to be delivered before or on the day you go home. See reablement after hospital for short-term help at home.
  • If you are at home: ask your council's adult social care team for a free needs assessment. You can ask for yourself, or a family member or carer can ask for you. You can also ask your GP, community physiotherapist or community nurse.
  • Be specific about what is hard: getting off the toilet, in and out of bed, the bath, the stairs, or walking around the house. An occupational therapist can then suggest the right item and check it fits you and your home.
  • Wheelchairs for longer-term use come through the NHS wheelchair service, usually after a referral from your GP or therapist. For short spells, a loan or hire is often quicker.

Waiting times vary. If you are struggling to manage safely while you wait, tell the team, because they may be able to prioritise you.

Route 2: charity loans and hire

  • The British Red Cross hires out wheelchairs across the UK for short periods, with delivery to your home in many areas. It does not need a GP letter. In some areas the NHS funds the hire, so check when you book.
  • Local charities, hospices, Age UK branches and shopmobility schemes sometimes lend or hire equipment. Your council, GP surgery or local Age UK may know what is available near you.
  • Specialist disability equipment hire companies also rent items such as wheelchairs, scooters and riser recliner chairs. Ask about delivery, collection and what happens if something breaks.

Route 3: buying, new or second-hand

Small items such as a long-handled shoe horn or a pair of grab rails may be cheaper to buy. Before you do, ask an occupational therapist or physiotherapist what would suit you. Living Made Easy, from the Disabled Living Foundation, has impartial information on thousands of products.

  • If you have a disability or long-term illness, you may not have to pay VAT on equipment designed or adapted for you. Ask the supplier about VAT relief before you pay.
  • Second-hand equipment can save money, but it may be worn, missing parts or the wrong size. Check frames and sticks for worn rubber ferrules, loose joints and bent legs. Ferrules can be replaced cheaply.
  • Be cautious with second-hand hoists, stairlifts, electric beds and riser chairs, which need proper fitting, servicing and safety checks. Ask about the service history.
  • Do not use a walking frame, stick or commode that wobbles, or one set to someone else's height without having it adjusted.

Using equipment safely

  • Ask the person who supplies it to show you how to use it, and to set walking aids to the right height for you. If your hands or wrists are painful, ask about different grips.
  • Clear a path and remove loose rugs where you will use a frame. A frame with wheels may need wider space.
  • Put a commode or urinal near the bed if night-time trips to the toilet are risky, with a light you can reach. See safer night-time trips to the toilet.
  • Equipment should help you keep moving, not replace it. Keep doing the exercises your physiotherapist gives you so you can rely on it less over time.

Giving equipment back

When you no longer need loaned equipment, contact the service that supplied it to arrange collection. Returned equipment is cleaned and reused for other people. If you still need it, tell the service rather than returning it, and ask for a review if your needs change.

When to get help

  • Call 999 after a fall if you cannot get up, have hit your head while taking blood thinners, have a new inability to bear weight, or severe hip or groin pain.
  • Contact NHS 111 or your GP the same day if you are suddenly much less able to move than usual, or have a hot, swollen joint with a temperature.
  • See your GP if you are struggling to wash, dress or get to the toilet, or are falling or nearly falling.

For family and carers

You can request a needs assessment on someone's behalf with their agreement, and you can ask for a carer's assessment for yourself. Help set equipment up, then let the person use it themselves as much as possible.

Common questions

Do I have to pay for equipment from the council?

Equipment and small adaptations are free if you are assessed as needing them. Larger adaptations may need a grant, which can be means-tested.

Can I get a commode or walking frame the same day?

Sometimes, especially if you are leaving hospital, but it depends on your area. Ask early, and say clearly if you cannot manage safely without it.

What if the equipment is not right for me?

Tell the service that supplied it. Do not keep using an item that feels unsafe or causes pain.
